NATIVE SKETCH / ENGINEERINGTASK 002 · 14 OCT 2026
Measured renderer comparison · macOS / Metal

Skia vs Vello GPU.
A workload tradeoff.

Skia is the stronger starting point for responsive drawing and navigation in this prototype. Vello GPU deserves to stay in contention for dense documents and heavy transparency.

Production renderer selection: OPEN
Recommendation

Use Skia for the next interactive integration experiment.

Keep Vello GPU as an active candidate. First optimize the application’s scene caching and presentation schedule, then repeat the comparison before committing permanently. The current app’s prototype painters remain unchanged.

Tested: Skia Ganesh/Metal (skia-safe 0.153.3) and Vello GPU Sparse Strips 0.3.0. This report compares pinned implementations on one Mac. It does not establish physical pen latency, displayed FPS, universal platform support, or the best performance either library can achieve.

New: native AppKit/Core Graphics measurements and app-size audit

Why the direction makes sense

Skia retains vector paths and changes the canvas transform during navigation. This Vello GPU adapter reprocesses pixel-space strips when the transform changes. Live updates rebuild scene geometry under the same declared policy.

Where the recommendation could change

If large retained documents or layered transparency dominate the product workload, Vello’s advantages become more important. A separate live-ink overlay, transform caching, tiles and different presentation scheduling could change both engines’ results.

Full occlusion, minimization, session, sleep or surface changes invalidate a run. These controlled conditions are distinct from the original matrix and from a normal production window.

Across all five original high-resolution native-paced pairs, Vello’s service p95 exceeds Skia’s by 22.38–27.54 ms for pan/zoom and 1.00–1.82 ms for live drawing. For 5,000 retained strokes, Vello is lower by 7.56–8.75 ms. Small, mixed light-scene differences should not drive selection.

04 / Engineering judgment

Pros, cons and integration costs.

Skia Ganesh / Metal

Best next interaction baseline

Advantages

  • Lower live-update and pan/zoom service costs in this implementation; sustained pan/zoom direction survives the guarded replay.
  • Retained vector paths allow inexpensive transform changes under the current policy.
  • Lower first-use service and process peak RSS than Vello for the 5,000-stroke fixture.

Disadvantages and risks

  • Much higher costs for high-resolution overlapping transparency; the disadvantage persists under guarded conditions.
  • Higher steady rendering costs for the retained dense scene.
  • Native C++ binary/build dependency. The minimal Metal prebuilt archive returned 404; unused JPEG/PDF features were enabled to consume a published package.
  • Cache strategy and production surface lifecycle still need integration work.
Vello GPU / Sparse Strips

Strong retained-scene candidate

Advantages

  • Lower steady costs for 5,000 retained strokes and high-resolution heavy transparency.
  • Substantially lower process RSS for the transparency fixture.
  • Rust/wgpu integration avoids the Skia C++ binary dependency, although it has its own resource and dependency constraints.

Disadvantages and risks

  • CPU strip reprocessing makes pan/zoom expensive with this adapter’s invalidation policy.
  • Live-update service costs are higher in the original paired trials.
  • Higher first-use service and peak RSS for the 5,000-stroke fixture despite lower steady costs.
  • Results apply to Sparse Strips 0.3.0, not every Vello variant or future caching strategy.

Packaging observations are concrete setup experience, not measured build-time or binary-size comparisons. Neither candidate has been independently optimized into a production drawing architecture.

Recommended next experiment

  1. Keep the shared Rust document and editing semantics. Preserve native controls and put renderer-specific work behind a narrow canvas boundary.
  2. Integrate Skia in one scoped interactive prototype. Measure live ink and navigation with a retained base scene plus transient ink overlay.
  3. Give both engines equivalent optimized policies. Explore dirty regions/tiles, transform caching and preparing CPU work before drawable acquisition.
  4. Repeat on agreed workloads and hardware. Check tail timings, first use, memory, visual quality and observable presentation. Add physical input-to-screen measurements before making latency claims.
  5. Decide with the owner. Weight real document sizes and platform requirements before choosing a production renderer. No automatic winner score or permanent commitment is proposed here.
05 / Costs beyond steady rendering

First use and memory change the picture.

Vello’s retained dense-scene advantage comes with a higher first-use cost in this fixture. Heavy transparency is the opposite: Skia uses substantially more whole-process memory.

RSS is not isolated renderer memory. It includes the AppKit host, both linked libraries, common fixture/image data, retained measurement rows and untimed readback/PNG output. Faster sustained processes store more rows. Unified CPU/GPU memory counters must not be added together.

Live initialization includes roughly one second of common geometry-identity precomputation. Finish-time Metal allocation is a snapshot, not peak residency. Physical footprint, GPU peak memory, energy consumption and final package size were not compared.

06 / Output fidelity

Geometry agrees; pixels are not identical.

The designer reviewed all eight fixture pairs at both captured resolutions. No visible correctness blocker was found: placement, pressure widths, stroke order, translucent interiors, curved clipping and image orientation agreed. Edge coverage and faint image-filtering differences remain.

Selected original 2560×1600, frame-599 comparison sheets below contain Skia and Vello outputs, an amplified RGB difference and descriptive statistics. They are embedded in this HTML and remain available offline. Difference magnification is 8×; pixel error is not an acceptance threshold.

07 / Product implications

One shared engine does not remove platform validation.

The evidence is macOS/Metal only. The following are integration directions and open checks, not completed port certifications or claims that either pinned renderer supports every target.

Planned native UI boundaries and required target evidence
Platform familyNative interface directionWhat this comparison leaves open
macOSSwift + AppKit; SwiftUI where control behavior fitsBoth candidates exercised on one Mac. Production surface lifecycle, pen latency, energy and wider hardware remain open.
iPhone / iPad / visionOSSwift + UIKit / appropriate native SwiftUI surfacesTarget builds, touch/Pencil or spatial input, Metal surface integration, memory budgets and sustained device thermals.
Apple TV / Apple WatchNative viewer-focused interface; device-specific previews may be appropriateRenderer feasibility and viewer policy must be checked per SDK. A desktop Metal result is not watchOS support evidence.
Android / ChromeOSKotlin + Android Views / standard Material controls where supportedAndroid distribution/runtime availability, GPU drivers, stylus, mouse/keyboard and resizable desktop windows. ChromeOS product/OS targets need confirmation.
WindowsC# + WinUI 3, calling shared RustNative composition/surface integration, GPU backend and driver validation, pen input and comparable measurements.
LinuxRust + GTK4 / libadwaitaWindow-system integration, Vulkan/driver coverage, input and desktop-specific behavior.
BrowserTypeScript + semantic HTML, Rust/Wasm canvas engineActual Wasm build/backend feasibility, WebGPU availability/fallbacks, browser input and package/startup cost.

This report does not verify “GooglebookOS” as a specific OS/runtime target. Confirm the product’s actual platform and distribution model before assigning it an Android, browser or Linux implementation path. Native controls and shared Rust semantics remain separate from the canvas renderer choice.

08 / Trust and reproducibility

What was tested, and what was not.

Exact candidates

Skia: skia-safe 0.153.3, Ganesh over Metal, upstream binding reference m153-0.101.2.

Vello GPU: vello_gpu 0.3.0 + vello_common 0.3.0, Sparse Strips CPU path preprocessing with GPU rasterization/compositing. This is not compute-centric Vello 0.8.0 or Vello CPU.

GPU access: wgpu 30.0.0, locked internals 30.0.1; Metal only.

Reference environment

Apple M2 Pro, 12 CPU cores, 16 GiB unified memory. macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), SDK 27.0, Rust 1.99.0, Swift 6.4. AC power; nominal 120 Hz display, backing scale 2.

Other desktop applications and OS services remained open. No concurrent agent builds, GPU experiments or native UI automation ran during measurements. Thermal observations recorded no warning; this does not prove absence of throttling.

Equivalent inputs, explicit policy

Both adapters consume real Rust Editor::render outlines, fill each whole stroke once with nonzero winding, and share geometry, traces, transforms and decoded image bytes. Both use the same Metal device/queue, BGRA8 offscreen target, final native blit and CAMetalLayer policy. There is no timed CPU readback.

Static vector resources are retained but rasterization occurs every frame. The common pipeline acquires a drawable before CPU scene preparation, so a CPU-heavy engine holds it during that work. Alternative overlap/scheduling was not tested. Both use analytic coverage at sample count 1, bilinear filtering without mipmaps, and numeric sRGB channels without linear-light conversion; this does not prove equal antialiasing quality.

How to read the measurements
MeasurementInterpretation
Service excluding acquisitionPer-frame service minus drawable acquisition. Includes synchronous backend waits; not pure CPU execution or input latency.
CPU frame-start intervalTime between consecutive CPU frame starts. Includes retirement backpressure and scheduling; not displayed FPS.
GPU timeline spanCommon begin marker before scene preparation through final blit GPU end. Includes CPU/queue gaps; not pure GPU execution. Do not sum with overlapping metrics.
p95 and variationNearest-rank process percentiles. Original chart medians summarize five process p95s, with min–max whiskers. No pooled-frame headline percentile or confidence interval.
Presentation callbacksPositive drawable presentedTime observations only. Gaps do not prove display outages or deadline misses.
Unsupported conclusionsNo physical pen-to-screen latency, true missed-display-deadline rate, GPU peak residency, energy, package-size or universal platform ranking.

Evidence coverage

  • Original: 320 primary + six sustained processes; 262,354 measured frames with GPU timeline spans. Eighteen calibration and sixteen separate quality processes are additional.
  • Guarded: 16 affected primary + six sustained processes; 94,158 GPU-timed measured frames. Valid complete pairs were assembled with source hashes. Failed/minimized attempts and an excluded unmatched run are preserved.
  • Calibration: ordered marker-off and sampler-off pilots had variable signs and magnitudes. No causal overhead estimate or correction was applied.

Verification and independent review

Integration revision 6e1fb271f68f6122108164ce515d871a59df9ed0 passed the repository and renderer checks: 26 production Rust tests, five experiment Rust tests, 24 Python analysis/recovery tests, native release build and Swift/Rust integration. The final interactive app rendered and restored its controls; this inspection is not performance data.

Independent reliability review reproduced original and guarded summaries and checked raw identities. A fresh reviewer’s lifecycle-observability finding led to the repair and separate reruns. Final evidence review found no unresolved actionable finding. Designer inspection covered native controls and matched output images.

Native host keyboard-event delivery was inconclusive; minimum-width resizing and dark appearance remain unverified. Browser CI passed for the PR, but it does not certify native GPU results. This HTML presents existing evidence; it introduces no new benchmark runs.
